body.text: Antibiotic resistance on track to kill 39 million people in coming decades, doctors warn
In short:
The peak body for doctors says increasing antibiotic resistance in Australia could threaten the foundations of modern medicine.
Antimicrobial resistance is considered one of the greatest global health threats.
What's next?
Doctors and experts are calling for governments to act and scale up solutions.
Millions of people are expected to die because of rising antimicrobial resistance over the coming decades, the peak body for Australian doctors has warned.

The latest Australian figures show reports of critical resistance jumped by more than 25 per cent in 2024 alone, and if current trends continue, antimicrobial resistance will cause the deaths of 39 million people globally by 2050 — more than the total deaths projected for all cancers.

Antimicrobial resistance is considered one of the greatest global health threats and occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites adapt to the medicines designed to treat them, most commonly, antibiotics.
It means infections become difficult or impossible to treat, which increases the risk of disease spread and death.
A new report released today by the Australian Medical Association (AMA) said the scale of the threat in Australia was rising and resistance was outpacing the national response.
AMA president Michael Bonning said antibiotic resistance was already having devastating consequences and threatened to undermine the foundations of modern medicine.

"When antibiotics and other antimicrobials stop working, it doesn't just make infections harder to treat, it also makes the medical procedures we now take for granted, from joint replacements to cancer treatment and caesarean sections, much riskier,"
he said.
The World Health Organization (WHO) last year warned resistance to essential antibiotics was "widespread, increasing and unevenly distributed".
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a similarly stark warning last month, saying drug-resistant germs caused an estimated 50,800 deaths in the country each year.
The latest figures show in 2020, more than 1,000 Australians died because of infections caused by five common antimicrobial-resistant bacteria.

Although antimicrobial stewardship, which is specialised programs to promote responsible use of antimicrobials in the health system, has reduced overall antibiotic use by about 21 per cent in the past decade, prescribing has risen in residential aged care.
Dr Bonning said such stewardship needed to be scaled up across hospitals, primary care and aged care, as well as agriculture and the environment.
"We know what needs to be done. What we need now is coordinated action from governments and proper investment to implement those commitments and turn plans into results," he said.
The AMA report also took aim at state and federal initiatives allowing pharmacies to prescribe antibiotics for urinary tract infections without a script from a GP.
It said evidence showed E. coli, which causes urinary tract infections, had developed resistance to Trimethoprim, an antibiotic available through some pharmacy prescribing programs.

A spokesperson for the Pharmacy Guild of Australia said suggestions that pharmacies were independently choosing which antibiotics to prescribe were wrong, as they followed the same therapeutic guidelines as doctors.
"Antimicrobial resistance is a whole-of-health-system challenge. The answer is strong antimicrobial stewardship by every prescriber …. not scaremongering and old turf wars," they said.
Only a 'handful' of new antibiotics being explored

Molecular biologist Amy Cain, who has dedicated her career to finding solutions for antimicrobial resistance, said the situation was getting increasingly "dangerous" and the world was "looking off a cliff".
"We're right on the cusp of an exponential increase of resistance and failure of our trusty antibiotics that we've had for so long not working,"
she said.
"I think anyone that's had a really nasty infection, especially one that hasn't responded to treatment, will understand how scary it is."

Dr Cain, who works to find new antibiotics at the Galleria Research Facility at Macquarie University, said there were only a "handful" of new antibiotics in the pipeline globally and urgent funding was needed to turbocharge development.

She said the pressure to develop new treatments fell heavily on academics and small research organisations, with pharmaceutical companies unmotivated to find breakthroughs as they did not stand to make significant financial gains from new antibiotics.
Dr Cain said tackling the problem must recognise the interconnectedness of human, animal and environmental health.
She said she was concerned about antibiotic use in agriculture and called on Australia to catch up to the European Union, which had banned antibiotics in animal feed.

A spokesperson for the Australian Centre for Disease Control, a national organisation set up after the COVID-19 pandemic, said it was committed to reducing resistance as a matter of national importance and the country's antimicrobial surveillance program was critical in the fight.

The surveillance program, called AURA, which analyses data from across the community to identify resistant infections and rates of antibiotic use, received more than $22 million in funding in 2024, they said.
